paras: The lynching of George Scott took place at Brazil, Indiana, on the night of December 11-12, 1880, when masked men took Scott from the Clay county jail and hanged him from a tree beside it. Scott, described in the press as 'a half-breed Indian and negro', was being held on a charge of assaulting the wife of his employer. No one was reported arrested, and the story ran as a brief wire item in papers across the country for more than a month.

According to an account credited to the Examiner, Scott had been hired by a Mr. Allison, who lived six miles from Brazil, to chop wood. The same account charged that while Allison was away Scott went to the house with an ax, overpowered Mrs. Allison, assaulted her in front of her three children and took a gold watch from one of them. A Batesville paper named the husband as Joseph Allison, 'a well-to-do farmer living in the eastern part of the county'. A Brazil dispatch to the Omaha Bee said Scott was captured at 'Marton', Indiana, and brought back to Brazil, where he was jailed.

The Cincinnati Commercial's Brazil special, dated December 12, reported that Scott 'was lynched last night by a party of masked men, who took him from the jail'. The fullest description, a special reprinted by the Memphis Public Ledger, said about 1,000 men gathered at the jail, which stood in an isolated part of the city, and a guard kept the crowd back while a leader and twenty chosen men went to the door. When the keys were refused, they battered the door open, overpowered the jailer and took his keys.

Scott resisted being taken from his cell and fought again in the jail yard, crying 'Murder!' and 'Mercy!', and was bruised on the head and body before he was overcome. He was led to a tree near the jail, the rope was thrown over a limb, and men pulling on it together hanged him. The crowd then dispersed, and the Examiner account likewise said the lynchers 'quietly dispersed'.

The coroner cut the body down the next morning and took charge of it. The Memphis account added that, 'although no secret was made of the matter, no one can be found who was there or who knows anything about it'. No report of an inquest verdict, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage.

Most papers carried the Commercial's one-sentence wire, starting with the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Washington Evening Star on December 13 and spreading over the next ten days to weeklies in Vermont, Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Kansas, Missouri and Arkansas. Headlines included 'Judge Lynch in Indiana', 'Lynched for an Outrage' and 'A Negro Lynched', and several papers printed the item in crime or news-summary columns without comment. Some versions called Scott 'a negro', and the Watertown Republican used a slur.

Other papers approved of the killing. The Omaha Bee headed its dispatch 'A Just Retribution', and the Memphis Public Ledger's account called Scott a 'miserable, groveling wretch' and a 'worthless dog' whose cries for mercy deserved no hearing. The Examiner account, reprinted by the Chickasaw Messenger of Okolona, Mississippi, on January 20, 1881, called Scott 'the brute'.

Accounts differ on the size of the mob: the Examiner described 'fifteen masked men', while the Memphis special described twenty men acting before a crowd of 1,000. The earliest dispatches said nothing of Mrs. Allison's death, but the Memphis account said Scott had 'outraged and murdered' her and that she died 'but a few hours before' the lynching. The Examiner said she 'died soon after', and the Batesville Guard reported only that it 'was rumored' she had died. The Examiner also placed the lynching on 'Saturday morning', against the Saturday night or early Sunday of the dispatches written in the following days.

bases: A party of masked men broke into the jail at Brazil, Indiana, took out a prisoner held on an assault charge and hanged him to a tree (A1, A9, A19).

Scott was taken from jail by a party of masked men, put at fifteen by one account and at twenty chosen from a crowd of 1,000 by another, and hanged without trial, as punishment for an alleged outrage on his employer's wife (A1, A9, A19).

The Cincinnati Commercial's Brazil special (A1, A4), a separate Brazil dispatch to the Omaha Bee (A3), the special quoted by the Memphis Public Ledger (A9) and the Examiner account (A19) all agree that masked men took Scott from the Brazil jail and hanged him.
